claim: Genetic defects in UNC-70 β-spectrin have been linked to movement-dependent axon fracture in C. elegans motor neurons.
source: Genetic defects in UNC-70 β-spectrin have been linked to movement-dependent axon fracture (Hammarlund et al., 2007) and buckling (Krieg et al., 2014) in C. elegans motor neurons and TRNs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Hammarlund et al., 2007).

claim: Genetic defects in UNC-70 β-spectrin have been linked to buckling in C. elegans TRNs.
source: Genetic defects in UNC-70 β-spectrin have been linked to movement-dependent axon fracture (Hammarlund et al., 2007) and buckling (Krieg et al., 2014) in C. elegans motor neurons and TRNs, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Krieg et al., 2014).

claim: Morphological distortions such as bends and kinks have been described in TRNs of animals carrying loss-of-function alleles of mec-17 α-tubulin acetyltransferase.
source: Additionally, morphological distortions in the TRNs such as bends and kinks have been described in animals carrying loss-of-function alleles of mec-17 α-tubulin acetyltransferase (Topalidou et al., 2012) and missense alleles of mec-12 α-tubulin (Hsu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Topalidou et al., 2012).

claim: Morphological distortions such as bends and kinks have been described in TRNs of animals carrying missense alleles of mec-12 α-tubulin.
source: Additionally, morphological distortions in the TRNs such as bends and kinks have been described in animals carrying loss-of-function alleles of mec-17 α-tubulin acetyltransferase (Topalidou et al., 2012) and missense alleles of mec-12 α-tubulin (Hsu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Hsu et al., 2014).

claim: No shape distortions appear in mutants lacking MT bundles in the TRNs.
source: No such shape distortions appear in mutants lacking MT bundles in the TRNs (Chalfie and Thomson, 1982; Hsu et al., 2014; this study—Figure 1A), suggesting that defects in MT bundles, but not their absence, cause shape distortions
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior work (Chalfie and Thomson, 1982; Hsu et al., 2014) and data from this study shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Defects in MT bundles, but not their absence, cause shape distortions in TRNs.
source: No such shape distortions appear in mutants lacking MT bundles in the TRNs (Chalfie and Thomson, 1982; Hsu et al., 2014; this study—Figure 1A), suggesting that defects in MT bundles, but not their absence, cause shape distortions
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that mutants lacking MT bundles do not show shape distortions, while mutants with defective MT bundles do.

claim: The e524 allele encodes a missense mutation, E2008K, affecting the linker region between the tetramerization domain and the 16th spectrin repeat of β-spectrin.
source: The e524 allele encodes a missense mutation, E2008K, affecting the linker region between the tetramerization domain and the 16th spectrin repeat of β-spectrin (Krieg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Krieg et al., 2014).

claim: The wy116 allele replaces threonine 409 with an isoleucine in MEC-7 β-tubulin.
source: The wy116 allele replaces threonine 409 with an isoleucine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and maps to a region in the C-terminal tail of MEC-7 β-tubulin thought to form the interface between α and β tubulins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The wy116 allele maps to a region in the C-terminal tail of MEC-7 β-tubulin thought to form the interface between α and β tubulins.
source: The wy116 allele replaces threonine 409 with an isoleucine (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and maps to a region in the C-terminal tail of MEC-7 β-tubulin thought to form the interface between α and β tubulins (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and draws on established knowledge about tubulin structure.

claim: TRNs in young-adult mec-7(wy116) animals were straight and lacked local bends and shape distortions.
source: As in wild type, TRNs in young-adult mec-7(wy116) animals were straight and lacked local bends and shape distortions (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The TRNs in mec-7(wy116);unc-70(e524) double mutants displayed large bends and kinks that were not found in either single mutant.
source: The TRNs in mec-7(wy116);unc-70(e524) double mutants displayed large bends and kinks that were not found in either single mutant.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Shape defects were largely absent in mec-12(e1607); unc-70(e524) double mutants that lack MEC-12 α-tubulin and fail to form 15pf MTs in TRNs.
source: Such shape defects were largely absent in mec-12(e1607); unc-70(e524) double mutants (Figure 1A and B) that lack MEC-12 α-tubulin and fail to form 15pf MTs in TRNs (Chalfie and Thomson, 1982).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B and a citation to prior work (Chalfie and Thomson, 1982).

claim: TRNs in ptl-1(ok621) null mutants were straight, lacked obvious shape distortions, and had D values close to zero.
source: As found in mec-7(wy116), TRNs in ptl-1(ok621) null mutants were straight, lacked obvious shape distortions, and had D values close to zero (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: In ptl-1(ok621);unc-70(e524) double mutants, the TRN axons exhibited large bends and localized helices, loops, and plectonemes.
source: In ptl-1(ok621);unc-70(e524) double mutants, by contrast, the TRN axons exhibited large bends and localized helices, loops, and plectonemes (Figure 1A, Video 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Video 1.

claim: Rescue of β-spectrin in epidermal cells reduced but did not eliminate buckling instabilities in AVM neurons.
source: Given that rescue of β-spectrin in epidermal cells reduced but did not eliminate buckling instabilities in AVM neurons (Krieg et al., 2014), we examined ptl-1(ok621);unc-70(e524) double mutants expressing wild-type UNC-70 β-spectrin in the epidermis from the oxIs95[epi::UNC-70] transgene.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Krieg et al., 2014).

claim: The defects in ptl-1;unc-70 mutants appeared at roughly regular intervals of 13 ± 0.5 µm along the axon.
source: The defects in ptl-1;unc-70 mutants appeared at roughly regular intervals of 13 ± 0.5 µm (mean ± s.e.m., n = 121 intervals in 10 neurons) along the axon (Figure 1) and were dynamic.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The shape defects in ptl-1;unc-70 double mutants were dynamic.
source: The defects in ptl-1;unc-70 mutants appeared at roughly regular intervals of 13 ± 0.5 µm (mean ± s.e.m., n = 121 intervals in 10 neurons) along the axon (Figure 1) and were dynamic.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Releasing axial tension via in vivo laser axotomy readily drove reorganization of coils and plectonemes in ptl-1;unc-70 double mutant axons.
source: Consistent with this prediction, releasing axial tension via in vivo laser axotomy readily drove reorganization of coils and plectonemes (Figure 1D, Video 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and Video 5.

claim: Evidence of rotation following axotomy was found in some cases, indicative of a release from a preexisting, twisted state.
source: In some cases, we also found evidence of rotation following axotomy (Video 6), indicative of a release from a preexisting, twisted state.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Video 6.

claim: The AVM axon is located along the ventral midline at a distance of z = 21.1 ± 6.5 µm from the neutral bending axis in wild-type control animals.
source: In wild-type control animals (Figure 2A), the AVM axon is located along the ventral midline at a distance of z = 21.1 ± 6.5 µm (mean ± s.d., n = 32 worms) and the ALM axons lie much closer to the neutral bending axis at z = 5.5 ± 1.7 µm (n = 15 worms).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The ALM axons lie much closer to the neutral bending axis at z = 5.5 ± 1.7 µm in wild-type control animals.
source: In wild-type control animals (Figure 2A), the AVM axon is located along the ventral midline at a distance of z = 21.1 ± 6.5 µm (mean ± s.d., n = 32 worms) and the ALM axons lie much closer to the neutral bending axis at z = 5.5 ± 1.7 µm (n = 15 worms).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The body bends that occur during movement are expected to deform the AVM axon four-fold more than the ALM axon.
source: If Euler's simple theory of mechanical stress in a bending cylindrical beam holds for C. elegans, then the body bends that occur during movement are expected to deform the AVM axon four-fold more than the ALM axon.
evidence: The claim is based on a theoretical prediction derived from Euler beam bending theory applied to the measured positions of AVM and ALM axons.

claim: Wild-type AVM axons undergo local contractions and extensions with up to 50% strain observed during normal locomotion.
source: Consistent with this idea and prior work (Krieg et al., 2014), wild-type AVM axons undergo local contractions and extensions with up to 50% strain observed during normal locomotion (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Video 7, as well as a citation to prior work (Krieg et al., 2014).

claim: The ALM axons show only modest changes in strain during movement in wild-type animals.
source: The ALM axons, by contrast, show only modest changes in strain during movement (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, and Video 8.

claim: In him-4 mutants, AVM lies along the ventral midline and ALM lies near the dorsal midline at z = 17 ± 2.6 µm.
source: Thus, in him-4 mutants AVM lies along the ventral midline and ALM lies near the dorsal midline at z = 17 ± 2.6 µm (mean ± s.d., n = 9 worms, Figure 2D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text and illustrated in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Both AVM and ALM axons generate similar local contractions and extensions during locomotion in him-4 mutants.
source: Measuring the relationship between neuron strain and body strain in him-4 mutants, we found that both AVM and ALM axons generate similar local contractions and extensions during locomotion (Figure 2E and F; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Video 9, Video 10).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Video 9, and Video 10.

claim: AVM and ALM axons have similar mechanical properties.
source: These findings suggest that AVM and ALM axons have similar mechanical properties and that axon position has dramatic effects on bending-induced mechanical stresses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that AVM and ALM axons respond similarly to mechanical stress when positioned at similar distances from the neutral bending axis.

claim: Axon position has dramatic effects on bending-induced mechanical stresses.
source: These findings suggest that AVM and ALM axons have similar mechanical properties and that axon position has dramatic effects on bending-induced mechanical stresses.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that axons at different positions experience different levels of strain during body bending.

claim: unc-70 β-spectrin mutant neurons have reduced axial tension.
source: Previously (Krieg et al., 2014), we showed that unc-70 β-spectrin mutant neurons have reduced axial tension and that the axons of AVM neurons in unc-70 mutants undergo buckling instability under movement-induced compressive, but not tensile stress (Figure 3A,B and C; Video 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Krieg et al., 2014) and data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C, and Video 11.

claim: The axons of AVM neurons in unc-70 mutants undergo buckling instability under movement-induced compressive, but not tensile stress.
source: Previously (Krieg et al., 2014), we showed that unc-70 β-spectrin mutant neurons have reduced axial tension and that the axons of AVM neurons in unc-70 mutants undergo buckling instability under movement-induced compressive, but not tensile stress (Figure 3A,B and C; Video 11).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Krieg et al., 2014) and data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C, and Video 11.

claim: Similar buckling defects are not observed in the axons of ALM neurons in unc-70 mutants.
source: However, similar defects are not observed in the axons of ALM neurons in these mutants (Figure 3A,B and C, Video 12).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3A, B, and C, and Video 12.

claim: The ALM axons are positioned close to the animal's neutral bending axis, so they are exposed to significantly smaller compressive stresses during body bending.
source: The simplest explanation for this discrepancy is that because the ALM axons are positioned close to the animal's neutral bending axis, they are exposed to significantly smaller compressive stresses during body bending.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential behavior of AVM and ALM axons in unc-70 mutants and their positions relative to the neutral bending axis.

claim: Both AVM and ALM exhibited buckling during locomotion-induced compression in him-4;unc-70 double mutants.
source: Indeed, both AVM and ALM exhibited buckling during locomotion-induced compression in him-4;unc-70 double mutants, consistent with the large strains experienced by both neurons in this animal (Figure 3E and F; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Video 13, Video 14).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and F, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Video 13, and Video 14.

claim: Peripheral axons are subjected to mechanical stresses in a manner that depends on their anatomical position within the tissue.
source: Collectively, these findings support the idea that peripheral axons are subjected to mechanical stresses in a manner that depends on their anatomical position within the tissue.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the differential responses of AVM and ALM axons to mechanical stress depending on their position relative to the neutral bending axis.

claim: ptl-1(ok621) mutant axons had significantly lower Young's moduli (E = 4.6 ± 0.6 kPa) than wild-type axons (E = 6.1 ± 0.3 kPa).
source: We repeated these measurements and compared wild-type axons (E = 6.1 ± 0.3 kPa, mean ± sem, n = 11) to those of ptl-1(ok621) (E = 4.6 ± 0.6 kPa, mean ± sem, n = 18) and mec-7(wy116) neurons (E = 4.3 ± 0.4 kPa, mean ± sem, n = 17) and found that both classes of mutant axons had significantly lower Young's moduli, in agreement with our hypothesis that mutations affecting the microtubule cytoskeleton lead to decreases in bending rigidity.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claim: mec-7(wy116) mutant axons had significantly lower Young's moduli (E = 4.3 ± 0.4 kPa) than wild-type axons (E = 6.1 ± 0.3 kPa).
source: We repeated these measurements and compared wild-type axons (E = 6.1 ± 0.3 kPa, mean ± sem, n = 11) to those of ptl-1(ok621) (E = 4.6 ± 0.6 kPa, mean ± sem, n = 18) and mec-7(wy116) neurons (E = 4.3 ± 0.4 kPa, mean ± sem, n = 17) and found that both classes of mutant axons had significantly lower Young's moduli, in agreement with our hypothesis that mutations affecting the microtubule cytoskeleton lead to decreases in bending rigidity.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claim: Axonal stiffness depends on both the actin-spectrin cytoskeleton and MT bundles.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that axonal stiffness depends on both the actin-spectrin cytoskeleton and MT bundles.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that mutations affecting either the actin-spectrin cytoskeleton or MT bundles lead to decreases in axonal stiffness.

claim: Simulated axons displayed multiple plectonemes at intervals of ~10–20 µm.
source: Similar to our experimental findings, simulated axons displayed multiple plectonemes at intervals of ~10–20 µm (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from numerical simulations shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: TRN axons will appear straight even when highly twisted, provided they have a sufficiently high bending stiffness and are held under axial stiffness.
source: These simulations predict that TRN axons will appear straight even when highly twisted, provided they have a sufficiently high bending stiffness and are held under axial stiffness.
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on numerical simulations using the DER model.

claim: Reducing either bending stiffness or end-to-end axial stiffness leads to the formation of localized helices for small values of twist and plectoneme-like supercoils at high levels of twist.
source: Reducing either bending stiffness or end-to-end axial stiffness leads to the formation of localized helices for small values of twist and plectoneme-like supercoils at high levels of twist (see Nizette and Goriely, 1999).
evidence: The claim is a prediction based on numerical simulations and is supported by a citation to prior theoretical work (Nizette and Goriely, 1999).

claim: α– and β-spectrin formed periodic structures in wild-type C. elegans TRNs in vitro with an average spacing of 197 ± 13 nm and 199 ± 10 nm, respectively.
source: In agreement with studies of actin-spectrin networks in mammalian and invertebrate axons and dendrites (D'Este et al., 2016, 2015; He et al., 2016; Pielage et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014), α– and β-spectrin formed periodic structures in wild-type C. elegans TRNs in vitro (Figure 5, Video 16) with an average spacing of 197 ± 13 nm and 199 ± 10 nm, respectively (p=0.64, Mann-Whitney test), suggesting that the spectrin tetramer resides at its fully extended contour length in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text and shown in Figure 5 and Video 16, as well as citations to prior work.

claim: The spectrin tetramer resides at its fully extended contour length in wild-type C. elegans TRNs.
source: In agreement with studies of actin-spectrin networks in mammalian and invertebrate axons and dendrites (D'Este et al., 2016, 2015; He et al., 2016; Pielage et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2013; Zhong et al., 2014), α– and β-spectrin formed periodic structures in wild-type C. elegans TRNs in vitro (Figure 5, Video 16) with an average spacing of 197 ± 13 nm and 199 ± 10 nm, respectively (p=0.64, Mann-Whitney test), suggesting that the spectrin tetramer resides at its fully extended contour length in these cells.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the measured spacing of α– and β-spectrin in wild-type TRNs.

claim: Periodic spectrin structures observed in GFP::SPC-1 α-spectrin transgenic neurons in vitro were eliminated upon addition of the actin depolymerizing agent Latrunculin A.
source: Periodic spectrin structures observed in GFP::SPC-1 α-spectrin transgenic neurons in vitro were eliminated upon addition of the actin depolymerizing agent Latrunculin A (Figure 5c) and by loss of UNC-70 β-spectrin (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Periodic spectrin structures observed in GFP::SPC-1 α-spectrin transgenic neurons in vitro were eliminated by loss of UNC-70 β-spectrin.
source: Periodic spectrin structures observed in GFP::SPC-1 α-spectrin transgenic neurons in vitro were eliminated upon addition of the actin depolymerizing agent Latrunculin A (Figure 5c) and by loss of UNC-70 β-spectrin (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: α-spectrin remained organized into periodic structures in unc-70(e524) mutants, but displayed a slightly shorter period of 188 ± 13 nm.
source: Interestingly, α-spectrin remained organized into periodic structures in unc-70(e524) mutants (Figure 5E), but displayed a slightly shorter period of 188 ± 13 nm (p=0.003, Mann-Whitney U-test; Figure 5F).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text and shown in Figure 5E and F.

claim: The 5% shorter period in unc-70(e524) neurons is consistent with the decreased axial tension found in these mutants in vivo.
source: The 5% shorter period in unc-70(e524) neurons is consistent with the decreased axial tension found in these mutants in vivo (Krieg et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the measured spectrin periodicity and is supported by a citation to prior work (Krieg et al., 2015).

claim: Loss of ptl-1 expression had no obvious effect on the distribution of α-spectrin.
source: Loss of ptl-1 expression, by contrast, had no obvious effect on the distribution of α-spectrin (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), which still formed periodic structures with a period similar to that observed in wild-type neurons: 195 ± 10 nm (n = 10, U-test, p=0.42).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Spectrin forms a periodic structure sensitive to axial tension, but not defects in the microtubule cytoskeleton.
source: Taken together, these observations indicate spectrin forms a periodic structure sensitive to axial tension, but not defects in the microtubule cytoskeleton.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that spectrin periodicity is affected by unc-70 mutations but not by ptl-1 mutations.

claim: The distribution of edge-to-edge distances between adjacent microtubules are well described by a log-normal distribution with a geometric mean of 9.8 nm for wild-type TRNs.
source: The distribution of edge-to-edge distances between adjacent microtubules are well described by a log-normal distribution with a geometric mean of 9.8 nm for wild-type TRNs (Figure 6Aii).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Aii.

claim: The MTs are organized into an approximately hexagonal bundle in wild-type TRNs.
source: The MTs are organized into an approximately hexagonal bundle, as demonstrated by 60°, 120°, and 180° being the dominant angles between three adjacent MTs (Figure 6Aiii, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Aiii and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: In mec-7(wy116) TRNs, the distribution of edge-to-edge distances was altered such that the geometric mean decreased to 4 nm, or about half the value in wild-type.
source: In mec-7(wy116) TRNs, by contrast, the distribution of edge-to-edge distances was altered such that the geometric mean decreased to 4 nm, or about half the value in wild-type (Figure 6Bii).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Bii.

claim: The variance in the distribution of edge-to-edge distances in mec-7(wy116) TRNs was nearly three-fold that found in wild-type.
source: The variance in this distribution was nearly three-fold that found in wild-type (σ2 = 32 and 89 nm2 in wild-type and mec-7(wy116) respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claim: A hexagonal arrangement of MTs was also detected in mec-7(wy116) axons with similar distribution of inter-MT angles to wild type.
source: Despite this, a hexagonal arrangement of MTs was also detected in mec-7(wy116) axons (Figure 6Biii) with similar distribution of inter-MT angles to wild type (p=0.2; Watson U2 for radially distributed data), although the 120° and 180° peaks seemed collapsed together in the histograms.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Biii.

claim: Individual MTs often separated from the main bundle and adjacent MTs often contacted one another in mec-7(wy116) mutants.
source: However, individual MTs often separated from the main bundle and adjacent MTs often contacted one another in these mutants (Figure 6Bi), situations that we have seldom if ever observed in wild-type TRNs (Bellanger et al., 2012; Cueva et al., 2012, 2007, 2007; Hueston et al., 2008; Richardson et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Bi and citations to prior work.

claim: MTs were closer together in ptl-1(ok621) null mutants than in wild-type axons.
source: Similar to mec-7(wy116) missense mutants, MTs were closer together in ptl-1(ok621) null mutants than in wild-type axons (Figure 6Di, Dii).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Di and Dii.

claim: The distribution of edge-to-edge distances in ptl-1(ok621) null mutants had a geometric mean of 6.7 nm and a variance of 81 nm2.
source: The distribution of edge-to-edge distances had a geometric mean of 6.7 nm and a variance of 81 nm2.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text.

claim: The hexagonal geometry of MT cross-sections was largely unaffected in ptl-1(ok621) null mutants.
source: Meanwhile, the hexagonal geometry of MT cross-sections was largely unaffected (Figure 6Diii) despite our observation that adjacent MTs often collapsed onto one another (Figure 6Di).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Diii.

claim: Adjacent MTs often collapsed onto one another in ptl-1(ok621) null mutants.
source: Meanwhile, the hexagonal geometry of MT cross-sections was largely unaffected (Figure 6Diii) despite our observation that adjacent MTs often collapsed onto one another (Figure 6Di).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6Di.

claim: mec-7 β-tubulin and ptl-1 tau mutants had fewer and shorter microtubules than wild type.
source: This analysis also revealed that mec-7 β-tubulin and ptl-1 tau mutants had fewer and shorter microtubules than wild type (Figure 6F and G; Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6F and G, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Bundle stiffness is expected to be proportional to the number of filaments in the bundle.
source: Given that bundle stiffness is expected to be proportional to the number of filaments in the bundle (Bathe et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2007), this finding suggests that bending stiffness is decreased in both of these mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work (Bathe et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2007).

claim: Bending stiffness is decreased in mec-7 β-tubulin and ptl-1 tau mutants.
source: Given that bundle stiffness is expected to be proportional to the number of filaments in the bundle (Bathe et al., 2008; Guo et al., 2007), this finding suggests that bending stiffness is decreased in both of these mutants.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that mec-7 and ptl-1 mutants have fewer and shorter microtubules.

claim: Mutants lack a spacer or linker molecule leading to a reduction in the cross-sectional area of the MT bundle.
source: The fact that neighboring MTs contact one another in mutant but not wild-type axons suggests that mutants lack a spacer or linker molecule leading to a reduction in its cross-sectional area.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that MTs contact one another in mutant axons.

claim: A decrease in area and in the number of cross-links is expected to decrease the bending stiffness of the bundle.
source: A decrease in area and in the number of cross-links is expected to decrease the bending stiffness of the bundle (Bathe et al., 2008; Tolomeo and Holley, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical work (Bathe et al., 2008; Tolomeo and Holley, 1997).

claim: Defects that reduce MT length, number, and inter-microtubule spacing also decrease the axon's bending stiffness.
source: Thus, we propose that defects that reduce MT length, number, and inter-microtubule spacing also decrease the axon's bending stiffness.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed structural defects in mutant MT bundles and their expected effects on bending stiffness.

claim: Outer MTs rotated and tilted away from the central axis of the bundle in ptl-1 and ptl-1;unc-70 mutants.
source: One of the most striking and consistent observations in the ssTEM datasets from ptl-1 and ptl-1;unc-70 mutants was that outer MTs rotated and tilted away from the central axis of the bundle (Video 17) in manner that generated a twist of the entire MT bundle.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Video 17.

claim: The pitch angle was small near the center and increased linearly with across the bundle's radius in ptl-1 and ptl-1;unc-70 mutants.
source: This approach yields an estimate of the pitch of the helical twist in the entire bundle and showed that the pitch angle was small near the center and increased linearly with across the bundle's radius (Figure 7D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Helical perversions were observed in twisted bundles, in which the MT bundle reverses between clockwise and counter-clockwise twists.
source: Notably, we also observed helical perversions in twisted bundles, in which the MT bundle reverses between clockwise and counter-clockwise twists (Figure 7D, Video 17).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D and Video 17.

claim: ptl-1 loss of function resulted in fewer, shorter MTs that were organized into a twisted bundle.
source: Thus, ptl-1 loss of function resulted in fewer, shorter MTs that were organized into a twisted bundle, findings consistent with the idea that ptl-1 mutant axons have both decreased bending stiffness and increased torque.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed structural defects in ptl-1 mutant MT bundles.

claim: ptl-1 mutant axons have both decreased bending stiffness and increased torque.
source: Thus, ptl-1 loss of function resulted in fewer, shorter MTs that were organized into a twisted bundle, findings consistent with the idea that ptl-1 mutant axons have both decreased bending stiffness and increased torque.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed structural defects in ptl-1 mutant MT bundles.

claim: The apparent diffusion constant for PTL-1 in living axons was 0.12 ± 0.1 µm2 s−1.
source: On average, the apparent diffusion constant for PTL-1 in living axons was 0.12 ± 0.1 µm2 s−1 (mean ± s.d., n= 47), which agrees with values reported for mammalian tau in vitro (0.17 ± 0.03 µm2 s−1; Hinrichs et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative measurements reported in the text and a citation to prior work (Hinrichs et al., 2012).

claim: Both the recovery rate and the mobile fraction of PTL-1 increased in mec-7(ok2152) β-tubulin null mutants and in mec-7(wy116) β-tubulin missense mutants.
source: Both the recovery rate and the mobile fraction increased in mec-7(ok2152) β-tubulin null mutants and in mec-7(wy116) β-tubulin missense mutants.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations described in the text.

claim: PTL-1 mobility was unaffected in unc-70(e524) mutants.
source: By comparison, PTL-1 mobility was unaffected in unc-70(e524) mutants (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The wy116 allele affects the affinity of PTL-1 for mutant MTs.
source: We favor the idea that the wy116 allele affects the affinity for PTL-1 since unc-70(e524) had no detectable effect on PTL-1 mobility (Figure 8D and E) despite having fewer MTs (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that PTL-1 mobility is increased in mec-7(wy116) but not in unc-70(e524), despite both mutants having fewer MTs.

claim: PTL-1 binds to MTs in vivo.
source: Together, these results support the idea that PTL-1 binds to MTs in vivo and that the T409I mutation in MEC-7 β tubulin interferes with PTL-1 binding to MTs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the FRAP experiments showing that PTL-1 mobility is affected by mutations in mec-7 β-tubulin.

claim: The T409I mutation in MEC-7 β tubulin interferes with PTL-1 binding to MTs.
source: Together, these results support the idea that PTL-1 binds to MTs in vivo and that the T409I mutation in MEC-7 β tubulin interferes with PTL-1 binding to MTs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the FRAP experiments showing that PTL-1 mobility is increased in mec-7(wy116) mutants.

claim: MTs were shorter in AVM neurons than in the ALM neurons in wild-type animals.
source: In accord with prior studies of wild-type animals, we found that MTs were shorter in AVM neurons than in the ALM neurons, on average (Figure 9D; Figure 9—figure supplement 1; Table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D, Figure 9—figure supplement 1, and Table 2.

claim: Mechanical stress may be a factor that limits MT length in wild-type axons.
source: Thus, mechanical stress may be a factor that limits MT length in wild-type axons, since AVM neurons undergo more extreme cycles of compression and extension than do the ALM neurons (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that MTs are shorter in AVM neurons, which experience greater mechanical stress than ALM neurons.

claim: Neither the e524 partial loss-of-function nor the s1502 null allele of unc-70 caused a further reduction in MT length or number in AVM neurons.
source: Neither the e524 partial loss-of-function nor the s1502 null allele of unc-70 caused a further reduction in MT length or number in AVM neurons, but both alleles were associated with a decrease in MT length in the ALM neurons (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: Both the e524 and s1502 alleles of unc-70 were associated with a decrease in MT length in the ALM neurons.
source: Neither the e524 partial loss-of-function nor the s1502 null allele of unc-70 caused a further reduction in MT length or number in AVM neurons, but both alleles were associated with a decrease in MT length in the ALM neurons (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D and E.

claim: The variance in the number of MTs was higher in unc-70(s1502) mutant ALM neurons than that in either wild-type or unc-70(e524).
source: The variance in the number of MTs was higher in unc-70(s1502) mutant ALM neurons than that in either wild-type (F-test p=0.01) or unc-70(e524) (F-test p=0.05; Figure 9F. Figure 9—figure supplement 1), but no difference in average values was detected (Figure 9E).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis reported in the text and data shown in Figure 9F and Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The increased variance in MT number in unc-70(s1502) mutants is an indication that some long MTs persist because mechanical stresses are decreased and other MTs are shortened due to the loss of actin-spectrin networks.
source: In light of these differences, we interpret the increased variance in MT as an indication that some long MTs persist in s1502 mutants because mechanical stresses are decreased in this genetic background and other MTs are shortened due to the loss of actin-spectrin networks.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed variance in MT number in unc-70(s1502) mutants and the expected effects of reduced mechanical stress and loss of actin-spectrin networks.

claim: MT length and number in unc-70(e542);oxIs95[epi::UNC-70] transgenic animals were similar to those of unc-70(e542) mutants.
source: We found that MT length and number in unc-70(e542);oxIs95[epi::UNC-70] transgenic animals were similar to those of unc-70(e542) mutants (Table 2; Figure 9D and E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Table 2 and Figure 9D and E.

claim: The epi::UNC-70 transgene appeared to restore MT length to nearly wild-type levels in unc-70(s1502) mutants.
source: However, the epi::UNC-70 transgene appeared to restore MT length to nearly wild-type levels in unc-70(s1502) mutants (Figure 9D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: The mutant β-spectrin present in unc-70(e524) animals acts in a dominant fashion and interferes with the mechanical stabilization that would otherwise result from the expression of wild-type UNC-70 β-spectrin in the epidermis.
source: One plausible explanation for this result is that the mutant β-spectrin present in unc-70(e524) animals acts in a dominant fashion and interferes with the mechanical stabilization that would otherwise result from the expression of wild-type UNC-70 β-spectrin in the epidermis.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the observation that the epi::UNC-70 transgene does not rescue MT length in unc-70(e524) mutants.

claim: The longer ALM MTs are more susceptible to bending-induced fracture than the shorter AVM MTs.
source: Together, these findings suggest that the longer ALM MTs are more susceptible to bending-induced fracture than the shorter AVM MTs.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that ALM MTs are shortened in unc-70 mutants while AVM MTs are not.

claim: The actin-spectrin network provides a lateral support that protects the MT bundle against deformation via both cell-autonomous and non-autonomous mechanical stabilization.
source: In addition, an analysis of MT length and number in β-spectrin mutants suggests that the actin-spectrin network provides a lateral support that protects the MT bundle against deformation via both cell-autonomous and non-autonomous mechanical stabilization.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the analysis of MT length and number in β-spectrin mutants.

claim: Shape defects in the TRNs of ptl-1;unc-70 double mutants were more pronounced for growth at 20°C than at 15°C.
source: Control experiments revealed that shape defects in the TRNs of ptl-1;unc-70 double mutants were more pronounced for growth at 20°C than at 15°C (Figure 10A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10A.

claim: Axons were smooth in the ptl-1;unc-70;mec-7(e1434) triple mutant following growth at 20°C, where MT assembly is defective.
source: Strikingly, axons were smooth in the triple mutant following growth at 20°C, where MT assembly is defective (Figure 10B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 10B.

claim: The formation of loops, twists, and plectonemes in mutant axons depends on intact microtubules.
source: In summary, these findings indicate that the formation of loops, twists, and plectonemes in mutant axons depends on intact microtubules, likely due to the induction of torque resulting from their assembly into twisted bundles.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that shape defects are suppressed in ptl-1;unc-70;mec-7(e1434) triple mutants at the restrictive temperature.

claim: Actin-spectrin networks provide tension in axons.
source: The picture emerging from this work is that actin-spectrin networks provide tension, MT bundles confer stiffness, and microtubule-associate proteins like tau minimize torque within MT bundles.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined experimental and theoretical results presented in the study.

claim: MT bundles confer stiffness in axons.
source: The picture emerging from this work is that actin-spectrin networks provide tension, MT bundles confer stiffness, and microtubule-associate proteins like tau minimize torque within MT bundles.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined experimental and theoretical results presented in the study.

claim: Microtubule-associate proteins like tau minimize torque within MT bundles.
source: The picture emerging from this work is that actin-spectrin networks provide tension, MT bundles confer stiffness, and microtubule-associate proteins like tau minimize torque within MT bundles.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined experimental and theoretical results presented in the study.

claim: Tension, MT bundles, and microtubule-associate proteins combine to protect axons from mechanical damage.
source: Together, these factors combine to protect axons from mechanical damage.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the combined experimental and theoretical results presented in the study.

claim: Simulations based on Euler-Kirchhoff theory revealed that the balance of tension and torque stabilizes axons and dendrites.
source: Simulations based on Euler-Kirchhoff theory revealed that the balance of tension and torque stabilizes axons and dendrites and show that plectonemes result when torque overcomes tension (e.g. Figure 4A.).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Plectonemes result when torque overcomes tension.
source: Simulations based on Euler-Kirchhoff theory revealed that the balance of tension and torque stabilizes axons and dendrites and show that plectonemes result when torque overcomes tension (e.g. Figure 4A.).
evidence: The claim is supported by numerical simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: UNC-70 β-spectrin forms an extended cytoskeleton similar to that in mammalian neurons.
source: Experimental observations show that UNC-70 β-spectrin forms an extended cytoskeleton similar to that in mammalian neurons (this study and D'Este et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2013) and is essential for maintaining proper axial tension (Krieg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from this study and citations to prior work (D'Este et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2013).

claim: UNC-70 β-spectrin is essential for maintaining proper axial tension.
source: Experimental observations show that UNC-70 β-spectrin forms an extended cytoskeleton similar to that in mammalian neurons (this study and D'Este et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2013) and is essential for maintaining proper axial tension (Krieg et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Krieg et al., 2014).

claim: PTL-1 tau has a MT-binding domain in its C-terminus and an intrinsically disordered N-terminal projection domain harboring dozens of glutamate/proline repeats.
source: Like other tau proteins, PTL-1 has a MT-binding domain in its C-terminus and an intrinsically disordered N-terminal projection domain harboring dozens of glutamate/proline repeats (Chung et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Chung et al., 2015).

claim: The glutamate/proline repeats in PTL-1 tau have been proposed to function as a polyelectrolyte brush.
source: These repeats have been proposed to function as a polyelectrolyte brush (Wegmann et al., 2013), to regulate the spacing between MTs in bundles and confer steric stabilization against aggregation (Chung et al., 2015; Goedert et al., 1996).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior published work (Wegmann et al., 2013).

claim: PTL-1 tau enables MTs to glide past one another during mechanical stress-induced compression and elongation.
source: Our data are likewise consistent with the idea that PTL-1 tau and related MAP2 proteins enable MTs to glide past one another during mechanical stress-induced compression and elongation.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed structural defects in ptl-1 mutant MT bundles.

claim: PTL-1 allows sliding of MTs in a bundle by preventing MT-MT contact during locomotion and thus friction and the generation of torque within the bundle.
source: We infer that PTL-1 allows sliding of MTs in a bundle by preventing MT-MT contact during locomotion and thus friction and the generation of torque within the bundle that would otherwise impart torsion to the neurite as a whole.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed structural defects in ptl-1 mutant MT bundles.

claim: The MT bundles structures observed in ptl-1 mutants are strikingly similar to bundles of twisted filaments predicted to assemble from chiral biological polymers.
source: The MT bundles structures we observe in ptl-1 mutants are strikingly similar to bundles of twisted filaments predicted to assemble from chiral biological polymers (Grason and Bruinsma, 2007), suggesting similar physical mechanisms account for formation of twisted MTs bundles in neurons.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the similarity between observed MT bundle structures and theoretical predictions, supported by a citation to prior work (Grason and Bruinsma, 2007).

claim: The observed torque is an emergent property of MT assembly that appears in the absence of PTL-1.
source: We propose that the observed torque is an emergent property of MT assembly that appears in the absence of PTL-1, which normally mediates long-range repulsion between adjacent MTs.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the observed torque in ptl-1 mutant MT bundles.

claim: In the absence of PTL-1, MTs twist around one another so as to maximize the cohesive energy of a chiral bundle.
source: In the absence of such repulsion, MTs twist around one another so as to maximize the cohesive energy of a chiral bundle.
evidence: The claim is a speculative explanation for the observed twisting of MTs in ptl-1 mutant bundles.

claim: This mechanism is expected to be independent of the number of protofilaments per microtubule.
source: Although all microtubules possess a helical surface lattice (Hunyadi et al., 2007), this mechanism is expected to be independent of the number of protofilaments per microtubule, and to apply to both the unusual 15-protofilament MTs present in C. elegans TRNs, and also to the more common 13-protofilament MTs found in mammalian neurons.
evidence: The claim is a speculative prediction based on the proposed mechanism for MT bundle twisting.

claim: MT bundles and actin-spectrin networks act synergistically to prevent shape defects.
source: In summary, we propose that MT bundles and actin-spectrin networks act synergistically to prevent shape defects, as a deficiency in both structures was required for the appearance of plectonemes.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that plectonemes appear only in double mutants affecting both the actin-spectrin network and MT bundles.

claim: Spectrin, microtubules, and tau are among the most abundant components of the neuronal cytoskeletal and these proteins are conserved in all animals, from C. elegans to humans.
source: Spectrin, microtubules, and tau are among the most abundant components of the neuronal cytoskeletal and these proteins are conserved in all animals, from C. elegans to humans (Baines, 2009; Findeisen et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Baines, 2009; Findeisen et al., 2014).

claim: The same mechanisms that protect C. elegans peripheral neurons against mechanical deformation may also protect axons in the mammalian central nervous system from damage caused by mechanical stress during daily life or during traumatic brain injuries.
source: The same mechanisms that protect C. elegans peripheral neurons against mechanical deformation may also protect axons in the mammalian central nervous system from damage caused by mechanical stress during daily life or during traumatic brain injuries.
evidence: The claim is a speculative extrapolation from the findings in C. elegans to mammalian neurons.

claim: Mechanical stress has been implicated in neurodegenerative disease.
source: Intriguingly, mechanical stress has also been implicated in neurodegenerative disease (Levy Nogueira et al., 2016; Wostyn et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Levy Nogueira et al., 2016; Wostyn et al., 2010).

claim: Pathological biomarkers such as loss of tau function and spectrin degradation are shared between mechanical stress-based brain disease and aging-related neurodegeneration.
source: Thus, it may not be surprising that pathological biomarkers such as loss of tau function (Puvenna et al., 2016) and spectrin degradation are shared between mechanical stress-based brain disease and aging-related neurodegeneration (Cai et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior published work (Puvenna et al., 2016; Cai et al., 2012).

claim: Defects in the genes encoding tau, spectrin, and microtubule isoforms expressed in the nervous system may sensitize axons to mechanical stress and function as risk factors in traumatic brain injury or neurodegenerative disease.
source: Indeed, this work suggests the intriguing possibility that defects in the genes encoding tau, spectrin, and microtubule isoforms expressed in the nervous system sensitize axons to mechanical stress and function as risk factors in traumatic brain injury or neurodegenerative disease.
evidence: The claim is a speculative extrapolation from the findings in C. elegans to human disease.
